keywords_en: criminal; fraud; second instance; High People's Court; Beijing; natural person; Criminal Law; determination of fraud amount; whether the sentence is too heavy; affirm the original judgment; illegal entry; use of altered passport; fraudulent cashing of traveler's checks after reporting loss
full_text_en:
Mohammad Imami — fraud

Defendant: Mohammad Imami, male, 25 years old, national of the Islamic Republic of Iran, arrested on May 23, 1988.

Defense Counsel: Yu Beiping, lawyer from the Beijing No. 5 Law Firm.

The People's Procuratorate of Beijing Municipality, Branch, charged the defendant, Mohammad Imami, with fraud and initiated a public prosecution before the Beijing Intermediate People's Court. The Beijing Intermediate People's Court conducted a public trial of the case on September 24, 1988, and found:

The defendant, Mohammad Imami, between November 1987 and March 1988, on four occasions illegally entered the People's Republic of China using altered passports: a passport of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan (passport number: B346131, original holder's name: Mohammad Ali Ibrahim) and a passport of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (passport number: 100719115601, original holder's name: Waib Abu Zwada). From December 12 to 14, 1987, at the Foreign Currency Exchange Office of the Bank of China, Beijing Jianguomenwai, Mohammad Imami, by imitating the signatures of the original owners on traveler's checks, on five occasions used 28 traveler's checks issued by American Express International, Inc. that had been reported lost or stolen (total face value of £2,300) to fraudulently exchange for RMB Foreign Exchange Certificates totaling RMB 15,552.16.

From January 7 to 9, 1988, the defendant, Mohammad Imami, using the same method, at the foreign exchange counters of more than ten hotels in Beijing, including the "Kunlun," "Xiyuan," "Great Wall," and "Beijing," on thirty occasions used 300 "VSA" traveler's checks sold by Arab Financial Services Company of Manama, Bahrain, that had been reported lost or stolen (total face value of US$30,000) to fraudulently exchange for RMB Foreign Exchange Certificates totaling RMB 110,543.58.

On January 8, 1988, the defendant, Mohammad Imami, using the same method, at the foreign exchange counter of the Beijing Hotel, used 15 traveler's checks issued by Swiss Bank that had been reported lost or stolen (total face value of CHF 2,000) to fraudulently exchange for RMB Foreign Exchange Certificates totaling RMB 5,490.51.

On March 18, 1988, the defendant, Mohammad Imami, still using the above method, at the foreign exchange counter of the Beijing International Hotel, attempted to use 15 traveler's checks issued by American Express International, Inc. that had been reported lost or stolen (total face value of US$1,500) to fraudulently exchange for RMB Foreign Exchange Certificates, and was caught on the spot.

In summary, the defendant, Mohammad Imami, at the foreign exchange counters of more than ten hotels in Beijing and at the Foreign Currency Exchange Office of the Bank of China, Beijing Jianguomenwai, on 37 occasions used traveler's checks that had been reported lost or stolen to fraudulently exchange for RMB Foreign Exchange Certificates totaling RMB 131,586.25. The majority of the illicit proceeds were squandered.

After the case was uncovered, the public security authorities also searched Mohammad Imami's luggage and found 115 traveler's checks that had been reported lost or stolen, issued by companies and banks from the United States, Australia, and other countries, with a total face value of US$9,300.

The above facts are confirmed by physical evidence, documentary evidence, witness testimony, and forensic science examination conclusions on file. The facts are clear, the evidence is reliable and sufficient, and the determination is fully established.

The Beijing Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 3, Paragraph 1 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China, which provides that any crime committed within the territory of the People's Republic of China shall be governed by the Criminal Law of China unless otherwise specially provided by law, held that the defendant, Mohammad Imami, disregarded Chinese law, illegally entered China multiple times, and engaged in large-scale fraudulent activities. His conduct constituted the crime of fraud as stipulated in Article 152 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China. In accordance with Article 30 of the Criminal Law, deportation may be additionally imposed on Mohammad Imami as a supplementary punishment. In accordance with Article 60 of the Criminal Law, the property of Mohammad Imami used in the commission of the crime and the illegal gains shall be confiscated and recovered.

Accordingly, the Beijing Intermediate People's Court, on November 2, 1988, rendered judgment as follows:

The defendant, Mohammad Imami, was found guilty of fraud and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment, with the additional supplementary punishment of deportation; the property of the defendant used in the commission of the crime that was seized was to be confiscated, and illegal gains of over 1,000 yuan in foreign currency were to be recovered.

The defendant, Mohammad Imami, refused to accept the judgment of first instance and appealed to the Beijing High People's Court on the grounds that the fraudulent acts found in the judgment were not committed by him alone and that the sentence was excessive.

The Beijing High People's Court conducted a public trial of the case on January 14, 1989, and held: The appellant, Mohammad Imami, illegally entered Chinese territory multiple times, and within Chinese territory used altered passports and traveler's checks that had been reported lost or stolen to engage in fraudulent activities of a huge amount. His conduct constituted the crime of fraud and, in accordance with Chinese criminal law, should be punished. After being brought to justice, Mohammad Imami, in an attempt to evade criminal responsibility, repeatedly fabricated lies to deceive the Chinese judicial authorities, and even appealed claiming that the fraud was not committed by him alone. Investigation confirmed that the facts of fraud found in the original judgment were clear, supported by witness accusations, by the appellant's own handwriting on entry-exit registration cards, hotel registration forms, foreign exchange certificate exchange slips (including names, nationalities, passport numbers), and by handwriting identification conclusions of the countersignatures on the traveler's checks, as well as by physical evidence including the altered passports of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and the traveler's checks that had been reported lost or stolen found in his luggage. The grounds of appeal were untenable, and the request for leniency was not accepted. The original judgment's conviction of the appellant, Mohammad Imami, was accurate, the sentence was appropriate, and the trial procedure was lawful. On January 30, 1989, in accordance with Article 136, Item (1) of the Criminal Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court ordered the dismissal of the appeal by the appellant, Mohammad Imami, and affirmed the original judgment.
